How Organisations Buy and Where to Focus

Before you sell to a company, you need to understand how a company decides. This module explains the buying group and the stages of an organisational purchase, the numbers that drive a B2B sales plan, and how to choose a short list of accounts worth your time.

**B2B** means business to business: you sell a product or service to an organisation (a company, school, hospital, NGO or government agency) rather than to one person for personal use. The organisation pays from a budget, the purchase must be justified to other people, and the people who use your service are often not the people who approve the payment.

In B2B sales you are rarely selling to one person: a group meets, discusses and decides.

Because several people are involved, the person who first replies to you is only your way in. A friendly HR officer can love your idea and still be unable to buy it. Your strategy is to find out **who else is involved, what each of them needs to hear, and in what order the decision moves**.
The roles in a buying group
**User:** the people who will work with your product or service every day. They care whether it is easy and whether it makes their work lighter.
**Champion:** someone inside the organisation who wants your solution to win and will sell it internally when you are not in the room. A champion has influence, not just enthusiasm.
**Economic buyer:** the person with authority to release the money. Often a finance director, managing director or head of department with a budget.
**Technical evaluator:** checks that your solution works with what they already have (IT, legal, quality, safety). They can say no, but rarely say yes alone.
**Procurement:** runs the buying process: supplier registration, comparing quotes, negotiating terms and issuing the purchase order.
**Blocker:** anyone who loses something if you win, such as a current supplier's friend or a manager whose team will change. Ignoring blockers is how good deals quietly die.

One person can hold two roles. In a small company the managing director may be the economic buyer and the user. In a bank, the same purchase could pass through six or more people. Your job is not to guess: you ask, politely and early, "Apart from you, who else will be involved in a decision like this?"

Each stage has different people and questions, so your actions should match the stage the buyer is in.

Buyers often go back a stage. A new finance director may reopen the requirements, or a budget freeze may stop everything at approval. When a deal stalls, ask yourself which stage the buyer is really in, not which stage you hoped they were in. If they are still exploring options, a detailed price list is too early; if they are comparing suppliers, a general introduction is too late.
Approval limits decide who signs

Most organisations have a **delegation of authority**: a written rule about how much each level of manager may approve. A department head might approve small purchases alone, while larger ones need the finance director, the managing director or a tender committee. Learn the limits early, because they tell you who the real economic buyer is for your deal size.
Worked example: who must sign a payroll outsourcing deal?

For example, Amina sells a payroll and HR administration service. Her contact is the HR manager of a food processing company in Ota, Ogun State, with about 180 staff. The prices and limits below are illustrative.
Amina's proposed fee is ₦300,000 per month. A one-year contract is ₦300,000 x 12 = ₦3,600,000.

She asks the HR manager how purchases of this size are approved. He explains that he can approve up to ₦500,000, the finance controller up to ₦2,000,000, and anything above that needs the managing director.
₦3,600,000 is above ₦2,000,000, so the managing director is the economic buyer, and the finance controller will review the numbers first.
She also learns that the IT officer must confirm the payroll system can export to their accounting software, and that procurement registers every new supplier.
Amina writes a simple map: HR manager (user and possible champion), IT officer (technical evaluator), finance controller (reviewer), procurement (process), managing director (economic buyer).

Amina now knows she must prepare a business case that the finance controller can defend to the managing director, not just a demo for HR. Without asking about the approval limit, she would have spent weeks pitching to someone who could not sign.
Ask about process, not power

Asking "Are you the decision-maker?" can embarrass people. Ask instead: "How does a purchase like this usually get approved here?" and "Who would want to be involved before it goes for approval?" You get the same information and keep your contact's respect.
Never go around your contact without telling them

Reaching the managing director behind the back of the person who helped you can destroy trust. Ask your contact to introduce you, or to bring the relevant people to a meeting, and explain why it helps them.

The numbers behind a B2B sales plan: deal size, win rate, cycle and coverage

Strong B2B sellers plan backwards from a target using four numbers. You will use them all through this course, so learn the words once here.
A person standing beside a rising bar chart
A sales plan is built from a few simple numbers that you track every week.
**Average deal size:** the typical value of one won contract, for example over its first year.
**Win rate:** of the qualified opportunities that reach a decision, the share you win. If you win 3 out of 12, your win rate is 25%.
**Sales cycle length:** the usual number of days from a qualified opportunity to a signed contract.
**Pipeline:** all open, qualified opportunities with their values. **Pipeline coverage** is the value of your pipeline divided by the target you must close from it.

A **qualified opportunity** is not any company you have messaged. It is an organisation with a real need you can solve, where you have spoken to someone involved in the decision and there is a realistic path to a purchase. You will learn a fuller qualification method in Module 2. Counting unqualified names as pipeline is the most common way B2B sellers fool themselves.
Working backwards from a target
From many accounts to a few wins
Target accounts
First meetings
Qualified opportunities
Proposals
Wins
Each layer is smaller than the one above, so the number of wins you need decides how wide the base must be.
Worked example: planning a year of corporate training sales

For example, Ifeoma runs a staff training business in Lagos that sells customer service and supervisory skills workshops to banks, insurers and logistics firms. All figures are her own illustrative planning numbers.
Target: ₦18,000,000 of new contracts in 12 months. Her average deal is ₦1,500,000.
Wins needed: ₦18,000,000 ÷ ₦1,500,000 = 12 wins in the year.
Her win rate on qualified opportunities is 25%, so she needs 12 ÷ 0.25 = 48 qualified opportunities in the year.
That is 48 ÷ 12 = 4 new qualified opportunities every month.

Quarter check: her quarterly target is ₦18,000,000 ÷ 4 = ₦4,500,000. At a 25% win rate she needs ₦4,500,000 ÷ 0.25 = ₦18,000,000 of qualified pipeline that can close this quarter, which is 4 times coverage.

Ifeoma's real weekly job is to create about one new qualified opportunity a week. If at the start of a quarter she has only ₦9,000,000 of pipeline that can close in it, she already knows she is likely to fall short and must act now, not in the last month.

Coverage of three to four times is a common planning habit, but the right multiple is simply 1 ÷ your win rate. With a 25% win rate you need 4 times coverage; with a 50% win rate, 2 times is enough. This is why improving your win rate also reduces how many organisations you must chase, which matters a lot when each opportunity takes several meetings and a written proposal.
Sales velocity: four levers, one formula

**Sales velocity** tells you how much revenue your pipeline produces per day. The formula is: number of open qualified opportunities x average deal size x win rate ÷ sales cycle length in days. It shows that you have four levers, and that improving any one of them raises revenue.

Notice that raising the win rate by five points and shortening the cycle by 15 days give the same result. That helps you choose. If buyers keep stalling at the approval stage, shortening the cycle (with a clear action plan agreed with the buyer) may be easier than finding more opportunities. If you lose often at the comparison stage, improving discovery and the business case raises the win rate.
Why cycle length changes your calendar

If your cycle is 90 days, the opportunities you create in January mostly close in April. Revenue you want in the third quarter must be in your pipeline by the end of the first half. Many organisations also plan budgets once a year, so learn each target account's budget season and be in conversation before it, not after the money has been allocated.
Use your own numbers, not someone else's

Win rates and cycle lengths vary widely by industry, deal size and country, so do not copy a figure from a blog. Use your last 10 to 20 qualified opportunities to calculate your own. If you are new, start with a cautious guess, then replace it with real data after one quarter.
Keep the definitions honest

If you count every enquiry as an opportunity, your win rate looks terrible; if you only count deals you were sure of, it looks wonderful. Write down what counts as a qualified opportunity and a decision, and keep using the same definition so your numbers mean something.

In B2B sales your time is the scarcest resource. A deal may take months and several meetings, so chasing the wrong organisations is very expensive. The answer is to decide, on paper, which organisations you serve best and then focus on a short list of **target accounts**. An account is simply an organisation you sell to or hope to sell to.
A person pointing at a target with selected customer profiles
Choosing a short list of the right accounts saves months of effort on the wrong ones.
Write an ideal customer profile

An **ideal customer profile (ICP)** describes the kind of organisation that gets the most value from your offer and is realistic for you to win. It uses **firmographics**: facts about the organisation rather than about a person. Look at your best past clients, or the clients you are best equipped to serve, and write down what they have in common.
**Sector:** for example private hospitals, secondary schools, logistics companies, microfinance banks.
**Size:** number of staff, branches, vehicles, beds or students. Pick the measure that drives your price.
**Location:** where you can deliver well, for example Abuja and nearby, or anywhere online.
**Situation:** the problem they are likely to have, for example paper-based records, high staff turnover, a new regulation.
**Ability to pay:** signs they have budget for your price level, such as being an established business with several branches.
Look for buying signals

A good fit is not enough; timing matters. A **buying signal** (or trigger event) is a change that makes an organisation more likely to need you now. Examples: opening a new branch, hiring many new staff, a new managing director, a merger, a new regulation in their sector, a public complaint about service, a job advert for the very role your service supports, or a published invitation to tender. Signals give you a genuine, specific reason to contact them.

Accounts with strong fit and a live signal get your personal effort; strong fit without a signal gets light, regular contact.
Score and tier your list

Give each account a score from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on a few criteria, multiply by a weight that reflects importance, and add up. Then sort into tiers. **Tier 1** accounts get deep research and personal outreach. **Tier 2** get lighter, regular contact. **Tier 3** stay on a list for later.
Worked example: tiering five healthcare accounts

For example, Halima sells a managed IT support service (help desk, network care and backups) to private healthcare providers in Abuja. She scores five accounts using weights: Fit 40%, Signs of need 30%, Access to people 15%, Ability to pay 15%. Names are shortened to letters.
Hospital B (60 beds, opening a second branch): Fit 5, Need 5, Access 3, Pay 4. Score = 2.0 + 1.5 + 0.45 + 0.6 = 4.55.
Diagnostic lab C: Fit 4, Need 3, Access 2, Pay 4. Score = 1.6 + 0.9 + 0.3 + 0.6 = 3.4.
Public hospital D (buys through tenders): Fit 4, Need 4, Access 1, Pay 3. Score = 1.6 + 1.2 + 0.15 + 0.45 = 3.4.
Fertility clinic E (advertising for an IT officer): Fit 4, Need 4, Access 4, Pay 5. Score = 1.6 + 1.2 + 0.6 + 0.75 = 4.15.
Rule: 4.0 and above is Tier 1, 3.0 to 3.9 is Tier 2, below 3.0 is Tier 3.

Hospital B and clinic E are Tier 1 and get a full account plan this month. Lab C and hospital D are Tier 2; for D she will watch for published tenders instead of cold outreach. Clinic A is Tier 3 for now.

The most important line is the **value hypothesis**: your best guess, in numbers, of what the problem costs the organisation and what your offer could change. It is a hypothesis because you have not confirmed it yet. You will test it in discovery (Module 3). Never present a hypothesis to the client as a fact.
Worked example: an account plan for a haulage company

For example, Ngozi sells a fleet maintenance scheduling and vehicle tracking service. Her Tier 1 account is a haulage company in Kano that moves goods for manufacturers. All figures are illustrative assumptions she plans to test.
Facts: the website lists about 40 trucks and depots in Kano and Lagos. A job advert seeks a fleet supervisor. A news item mentions a new contract with a beverage company.
Buying group (from LinkedIn): managing director, operations manager, fleet supervisor (vacant), finance manager, and a procurement officer.
Hypothesis: if each truck loses about 2 days a month to unplanned breakdowns, that is 40 x 2 = 80 truck-days lost each month.
If one truck-day of work earns about ₦150,000 (to confirm), the revenue at risk is 80 x ₦150,000 = ₦12,000,000 a month.
Alternatives: their current mechanic arrangement, a competing tracking provider, or hiring the supervisor and doing nothing else.
Next actions: ask a mutual contact for an introduction to the operations manager by Friday; prepare five discovery questions on breakdowns; read the beverage company's delivery requirements.

Ngozi walks into her first meeting knowing the company's situation and with a specific question to test: "How many days a month do trucks spend off the road unexpectedly?" If the true figure is much lower, she revises the plan instead of pushing a weak case.

Also note what you could not find. If you cannot tell who approves IT or operations spending, or whether they already use a competitor, write it as an open question. A plan with three honest question marks is more useful than a plan filled with guesses, because it tells you exactly what to ask your first contact.
Recording it in a CRM

A **CRM** (customer relationship management tool) stores accounts, contacts, conversations and opportunities in one place, so nothing depends on your memory. Free tiers of tools such as HubSpot CRM or Zoho CRM work well, and a carefully organised Google Sheet is acceptable when you are starting. What matters is the structure, not the brand.
**Account record:** legal name, sector, size, location, tier, signals, link to the account plan.
**Contact records:** name, role, buying group role (user, champion, economic buyer and so on), how they prefer to be contacted, date of last contact.
**Opportunity record:** what you are proposing, value, stage, expected close date, next step with a date.
**Activity log:** a short note after every call or meeting: what you learned, what was agreed, what happens next.
Treat contact details as personal data

Names, phone numbers and emails of people at a company are personal data. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for collecting and using it. In practice: collect only work details you need, record where each came from, keep your CRM password-protected with two-step login, never buy or share contact lists, and remove a person promptly when they ask you to stop contacting them.
Research has a time limit

Set a timer. For a Tier 1 account, about an hour of research is usually enough to write a useful plan. Gaps are fine: they become your discovery questions. Endless research is often a way of avoiding the first conversation.

Decide when to disqualify an opportunity

Once an account becomes a real opportunity, you need a way to know where it truly stands. Many sellers move a deal to "proposal" because they sent a proposal. A stronger habit is to move a deal forward only when the **buyer** has done something that proves progress. These proofs are called **exit criteria**.

Qualify with MEDDICC

BANT (budget, authority, need, timing) is a quick first filter. For complex deals, many B2B teams use **MEDDICC**, a checklist of seven things you should know. Each letter is a question you keep answering as the deal develops.
**Metrics:** what measurable result does the buyer want, in their own numbers?
**Economic buyer:** who can release the money, and have you met them or their trusted delegate?
**Decision criteria:** what will they judge suppliers on: price, features, support, references, local presence?
**Decision process:** what steps, people and dates lead to a signature?
**Identify pain:** what is the problem, why does it matter now, and what happens if nothing changes?
**Champion:** who inside wants you to win and has the influence to help?
**Competition:** who else are they considering, including doing nothing or building it themselves?

Score each letter as known, partly known or unknown. Unknown letters are not failures: they are your next questions. But an opportunity at the negotiation stage with an unknown economic buyer or no champion is at real risk, however warm the conversations feel.

Keep MEDDICC as a private planning tool, not a script to read aloud. You fill it in by listening during normal conversations: the metrics come from discovery, the decision process from asking how purchases are approved, the competition from asking what else they are considering. Update the scores after every meeting so the gaps are always visible.
The mutual action plan

A **mutual action plan** is a short, shared list of the steps both sides will take to reach the buyer's goal, with owners and dates. You build it with your champion, working backwards from the date the buyer needs the result. It turns a vague "we'll get back to you" into a timetable both sides agreed to.

22 Jan: demo to finance
5 Feb: business case review
12 Feb: MD approval
19 Feb: contract signed
25 Mar: first live payroll
Each date depends on the one before it, so a slip early on moves the go-live date.
Worked example: a mutual action plan for a payroll deal

For example, Amina from Module 1 is selling her payroll service to the food processing company. The HR manager (her champion) says they want the new system running for the March payroll on 25 March. Dates are illustrative.
Amina asks what must happen before a live payroll: staff data moved, a test run alongside the old system, and a signed contract.
She allows about three weeks to load the records of 180 staff (20 February to 10 March) and ten days for a side-by-side test run (11 to 20 March).
So the contract must be signed by 19 February. From 19 February to 25 March is 34 days, about five weeks.

Working backwards: MD approval by 12 February, business case reviewed with the finance controller by 5 February, IT confirms the export to their accounting software by 29 January, demo to finance and IT by 22 January.
Each step gets an owner: Amina (demo, business case, data loading), HR manager (booking meetings), IT officer (export check), finance controller (review), procurement (supplier registration).
She shares the plan by email and asks the HR manager to correct anything unrealistic.

A **forecast** is your honest prediction of how much revenue will close in a period. Managers and business owners use it to plan hiring, stock and cash. If you work alone, it tells you whether you need to create more pipeline now. A forecast built on hope causes real damage: unpaid salaries, wasted stock, broken promises.
A person reviewing charts that project future results
A good forecast is built from evidence in each deal, not from how confident you feel.
Weighted pipeline

Give each stage a probability of closing, then multiply each deal's value by its stage probability. Start with your own history if you have it; if not, start cautiously and adjust each quarter. The probabilities below are illustrative, not industry standards.
Worked example: Ifeoma's quarter forecast

For example, Ifeoma (the training business from Module 1) has a quarterly target of ₦4,000,000 and five open opportunities expected to close this quarter. Her stage probabilities: Qualified 10%, Discovery complete 25%, Proposal reviewed 50%, Negotiation 75%, Verbal yes 90%.
Deal 1, insurer, ₦2,400,000 at Proposal reviewed: 2,400,000 x 0.50 = ₦1,200,000.
Deal 2, logistics firm, ₦1,800,000 at Negotiation: 1,800,000 x 0.75 = ₦1,350,000.
Deal 3, microfinance bank, ₦3,000,000 at Discovery complete: 3,000,000 x 0.25 = ₦750,000.
Deal 5, school group, ₦1,500,000 at Qualified: 1,500,000 x 0.10 = ₦150,000.
Commit (deals at Negotiation or Verbal yes): ₦1,800,000 + ₦900,000 = ₦2,700,000.

The weighted figure (₦4,260,000) looks above target, but only ₦2,700,000 is close to certain. Ifeoma reports a commit of ₦2,700,000 and a best case of ₦4,260,000, and she focuses this month on moving the insurer (Deal 1) to negotiation by confirming its economic buyer.
**Commit:** deals you would stake your reputation on closing this period.
**Best case:** commit plus deals that could close if the next steps go well.
**Pipeline:** everything else that is qualified but not expected this period.

Check your forecast against reality each quarter. If deals you placed at Proposal reviewed actually closed about a third of the time, not half, lower that stage to around 35% next quarter. Also watch **slipped deals**: opportunities whose close date has been pushed back two or more times. Repeated slipping usually means a missing piece, often no real economic buyer or no urgency, so treat those deals as best case at most until the gap is filled.

Remember that a signed contract is not yet money in the bank. Organisations usually pay on agreed terms, for example 30 days after receiving a correct invoice, and some only after a purchase order and a delivery note match. If you are planning cash rather than sales, add a separate column for when you expect payment, based on the payment terms in each contract.
The deal review

A **deal review** is a 10 to 15 minute look at one important opportunity, with a manager, a colleague or yourself using a written checklist. The aim is to find risk early and agree the next action, not to judge the seller.

Win/loss reviews

After each decision, win or lose, ask the buyer for 15 minutes of honest feedback. Buyers are more likely to agree if you ask respectfully and promise not to argue. Ask: what problem were you solving, what alternatives did you consider, what nearly made you choose differently, and what could we have done better? Record the answers in the CRM under a few fixed reason codes such as price, fit, timing, relationship, competitor, or no decision.

After 20 decisions you have patterns. For example, if Ifeoma won 6 of 20 (a 30% win rate) and 8 of her 14 losses were marked "no decision", her real competitor is the status quo, so she should strengthen the cost-of-inaction part of her discovery and business case rather than cut her price.
Do not inflate or hide

Two common forecasting habits damage trust: inflating (calling hopeful deals commit) and sandbagging (hiding likely deals to look good later). Both make planning impossible for the people who depend on your numbers. Report what the evidence supports, and explain changes plainly.

**Discovery** is the part of the sale where you learn the buyer's situation before proposing anything. In large B2B sales, one widely used method is **SPIN**, developed by Neil Rackham and the Huthwaite research team after observing tens of thousands of real sales calls. Huthwaite describes the research as observing more than 35,000 business-to-business sales interactions. SPIN names four kinds of question, asked roughly in order.
Two people in a structured conversation across a table
Good discovery feels like a focused business conversation, not an interrogation or a pitch.
The SPIN question sequence
Situation: facts and context
Problem: difficulties and dissatisfaction
Implication: consequences and cost
Need-payoff: value of solving it
Each question type builds on the last, so the buyer, not you, describes why change is worth paying for.
Type
Purpose
Example question
Situation
Understand facts you could not find in research. Keep these few: too many bore senior people.
How do you handle IT support today, in-house or through a vendor?
Problem
Find difficulties and dissatisfaction.
Where does the current setup cause you the most trouble?
Implication
Explore the consequences, so the problem feels as big as it really is.
When the records system goes down, what happens at the billing desk?
Need-payoff
Let the buyer say what solving it would be worth.
If outages became rare and short, what would that free up for you?

Implication questions are the heart of a complex sale. Most buyers can name a problem, but they have not added up what it costs. When they work out the cost themselves, in their own numbers, the figure belongs to them, and it becomes the foundation of your business case.
Worked example: putting a number on IT outages
For example, Halima (the IT support provider from Module 1) meets the finance manager and the IT officer at Hospital B. The numbers are the hospital's own estimates in this illustrative case.
Situation: the hospital has one IT officer, an external technician called when things break, and an electronic records and billing system.
Problem: the IT officer says the system goes down about 3 times a month, for about 4 hours each time.

Implication: that is 3 x 4 = 12 hours of downtime a month. Halima asks what happens to billing. The finance manager says the desk handles about ₦250,000 of bills an hour, written on paper during outages and posted later.

So about 12 x ₦250,000 = ₦3,000,000 of bills a month go through the paper route. She asks how much of that is never collected. The finance manager estimates about 10%, which is ₦300,000 a month, or ₦3,600,000 a year.

Need-payoff: "If outages dropped to one short one a month, what would that mean for your team?" The finance manager answers that most of that leakage would stop and his staff would stop working evenings to re-enter bills.
Halima leaves with a cost of the problem stated by the buyer (about ₦3,600,000 a year in uncollected bills, plus overtime), which she will use in her business case in the next lesson.
Different people, different questions
**Medical director or managing director:** risk, reputation and strategy. "How do outages affect patient care and the second branch opening?"
**Finance:** money and predictability. "What do unplanned repairs cost across a year?"
**IT officer:** workload and control. "Which tasks take most of your week that you would rather hand over?" Reassure them that the service supports them rather than replacing them.
**Procurement:** process. "What documents and approvals do new suppliers need here?"

Listen more than you talk. A useful habit is to pause after each answer and ask one follow-up such as "Can you give me a recent example?" or "How often does that happen?" Take notes in the buyer's words. Do not jump to your solution the moment a problem appears; you will lose the chance to understand its size.

Plan who you need to meet. One person rarely knows every number. In Halima's case the IT officer knew the outage pattern and the finance manager knew the billing figures, so meeting both together produced a cost neither could have given alone. If you can only meet one person, ask them to check a figure with a colleague and send it to you afterwards.

Before ending, summarise aloud: "Let me check I have this right..." and read back the key problems and numbers.
Agree the next step and date, and who else should join it.
Within 24 hours, send a short written recap: their situation, the problems and costs they described, what they want to achieve, and the agreed next step.
Invite corrections. A corrected recap is a gift: it shows exactly what matters to them.
Do not manipulate the numbers

Implication questions help buyers see real costs. They must never be used to frighten people with exaggerated risks or to push them into a figure they do not believe. If the buyer's estimate is small, accept it. A case built on inflated numbers collapses when finance checks it, and so does your reputation.

A **business case** is the document your champion takes into the approval meeting when you are not there. It must answer one question in the economic buyer's language: is the money better spent on this than kept or used elsewhere? It uses the numbers from discovery, not your marketing claims.
A person holding a signed contract with a check mark
A clear business case and fair terms lead to a contract both sides are glad to sign.
Three numbers finance will look for
**Total cost:** everything the buyer pays in the period, including one-time setup and recurring fees.
**Return on investment (ROI):** (benefits minus cost) ÷ cost, shown as a percentage.
**Payback period:** how long until the cumulative benefits cover the cost.
Worked example: Halima's business case for Hospital B

For example, Halima proposes managed IT support at ₦350,000 a month plus a one-time setup fee of ₦600,000. Benefits use the hospital's own estimates from discovery; the percentages are assumptions agreed with the finance manager. All figures are illustrative.
Benefit 1, less uncollected billing: the hospital loses about ₦3,600,000 a year; if 80% of that is recovered, that is ₦2,880,000.
Benefit 2, emergency technician callouts replaced: about ₦150,000 a month x 12 = ₦1,800,000.
Benefit 3, overtime avoided: about 40 hours a month at ₦2,500 an hour = ₦100,000 a month, or ₦1,200,000 a year.
Payback: monthly benefit is ₦5,880,000 ÷ 12 = ₦490,000; minus the ₦350,000 fee leaves ₦140,000 a month to repay the ₦600,000 setup. 600,000 ÷ 140,000 is about 4.3, so payback comes during month 5.
Cautious case: if only 40% of the billing loss is recovered (₦1,440,000), total benefit is ₦4,440,000 and year one shows a loss of ₦360,000.

Halima shows both cases honestly. The finance manager sees that the decision depends mainly on the billing recovery, so they agree to a 90-day review of outage hours. Showing the cautious case made the proposal more credible, not less.
Working with procurement

Procurement's job is to get good value, fair competition and proper records. Treat them as part of the buying group, not as an obstacle. Ask early what they need. Organisations commonly ask new suppliers for company registration documents from the CAC, tax details, bank details on letterhead, a company profile and references, but every buyer's list is different, so ask for theirs.
**Request for quotation (RFQ):** the buyer knows what they want and asks for prices. Answer exactly what is asked, on time.
**Request for proposal (RFP):** the buyer describes a need and asks how you would meet it. Your discovery work and business case matter most here.

**Tender:** a formal, rule-based competition. For federal government purchases in Nigeria, the Public Procurement Act 2007 applies and the Bureau of Public Procurement keeps a database of registered contractors and service providers. Follow every instruction; missing documents can disqualify an otherwise strong bid.
Stay clean in procurement

Never offer gifts, cash or a "percentage" to anyone to influence a purchase, and walk away if one is requested. Beware of fake tender notices and "registration fees" sent from personal email accounts: confirm any tender on the buyer's official website or by phoning their published number, and never pay to receive a contract.
Negotiation: know your walk-away point and trade

In the book Getting to Yes, Roger Fisher and William Ury introduced the idea of a **BATNA**: your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If this deal fails, what will you do instead? A strong alternative (other good opportunities in your pipeline) lets you stay calm. Before any negotiation, write your BATNA, your ideal outcome and your walk-away point.
Two ways to answer a discount request
Discount-led
Value-led trade
Cuts price straight away
Teaches buyer to push harder
Reduces your margin
Nothing gained in return
Asks what matters to them
Gives only in exchange
Protects your margin
Strengthens the relationship
Every concession should buy you something, such as a longer contract or faster payment.
Worked example: a discount request from procurement
For example, after approval, Hospital B's procurement officer asks Halima for 10% off the ₦350,000 monthly fee.
10% off a year of fees would be ₦4,200,000 x 10% = ₦420,000 given away for nothing.
Halima asks what is driving the request. The officer says the budget line is tight this year.
She offers a trade: 5% off (₦350,000 x 0.95 = ₦332,500 a month) if the hospital signs for 24 months and pays within 14 days of each invoice.
Her yearly fee becomes ₦332,500 x 12 = ₦3,990,000, a reduction of ₦210,000, but she secures two years of work instead of one and faster payment.
Procurement gets a saving to report, and Halima gets security and cash flow. Both sides gained something, which is the aim of a trade.

Show a cautious scenario: it makes the case more believable.

Understanding commission plans
**Base pay:** the fixed salary or retainer, paid whatever the results.
**Variable pay:** commission or bonus tied to results.
**On-target earnings (OTE):** base plus variable if you hit exactly 100% of quota.
**Quota:** the revenue or activity target for a period.
**Accelerator:** a higher commission rate on revenue above quota.
**Clawback:** commission you must return if the client cancels or does not pay. Check whether commission is paid on signed contracts or on cash collected.
Worked example: reading a commission plan

For example, Bisi is offered an account executive role. The figures are illustrative, not market rates: base pay ₦400,000 a month, target commission ₦200,000 a month, quarterly quota ₦12,000,000, commission of 5% on collected revenue up to quota and 8% above it.
In one quarter she collects ₦15,000,000 from her clients.
Commission up to quota: ₦12,000,000 x 5% = ₦600,000.
Total quarterly commission: ₦600,000 + ₦240,000 = ₦840,000.

At exactly quota she would earn ₦600,000 in quarterly commission, which matches the ₦200,000 monthly target. By beating quota by ₦3,000,000 she earns ₦840,000. Before signing, Bisi asks how quotas were set, what share of the team reached them last year, and how clawbacks work.

Notice how much the details matter. If commission is paid on cash collected, a client who pays 60 days late delays your pay too. If quotas rise every quarter regardless of the market, OTE becomes harder to reach. Ask for the plan document, read the definitions of quota, collected revenue and clawback, and run your own calculations at 80%, 100% and 120% of quota before you accept.

If you sell for several small companies on contract, agree in writing exactly what you do (for example research and qualified meetings only, or the full cycle to signature), the fixed monthly fee for your time, any performance bonus, how a qualified meeting or a closed deal is defined, and who owns the contact data and CRM records when the contract ends. For foreign clients, agree working hours across time zones and how you will be paid before you start.
Commission-only offers

Be careful with roles that pay only commission, especially from companies you cannot verify, or any role that asks you to pay a fee to start. Confirm the company's registration, speak to someone who has worked there, and get the plan in writing before you begin.

Why this matters
Selling to a group, not a person
B2B means selling to organisations
A group decides, over weeks or months
The user often cannot approve payment
Your time is the scarcest resource
B2B means business to business. You sell to an organisation, like a company, school, hospital or NGO, not to one person for personal use.
A group decides, and it takes weeks or months, because of meetings, budgets and approvals.
The people who use your service are often not the people who approve the payment. A friendly HR officer can love your idea and still be unable to buy it.
And deals take months, so choose your organisations carefully.
The buying group
Who is involved in the decision
User: works with it every day
Champion: sells it inside for you
Economic buyer: releases the money
Technical evaluator: checks it fits
Procurement: runs the buying process
Blocker: loses something if you win
The user works with your product every day, and cares whether it makes the work lighter.
A champion wants you to win and sells your solution when you are not in the room.
The economic buyer has the authority to release the money.
The technical evaluator checks that it works with what they already have. They can say no, but rarely say yes alone.
Procurement registers suppliers, compares quotes and issues the purchase order, often called an LPO in Nigeria.
And a blocker loses something if you win. Ignoring blockers is how good deals quietly die.

Who must sign Amina's deal?
For example, Amina sells a payroll and HR service to a food company in Ota, with about 180 staff.

Most organisations have a written rule on how much each manager may approve. It tells you who really signs.
For example, Amina's contact is the HR manager of a food company in Ota.
Her fee is 300,000 naira a month, so a one-year contract is 3,600,000 naira.
She asks how purchases this size are approved. The HR manager can approve up to 500,000 naira, and the finance controller up to 2,000,000.
So the managing director is the economic buyer, and the finance controller reviews the numbers first. Amina must prepare a business case they can defend, not just a demo for HR.
Ask well
Find the approval path politely
Ask this
How is a purchase like this approved?
Who else would want to be involved?
Ask your contact to introduce you
Avoid this
Are you the decision-maker?
Guessing who decides
Going around your contact
Ask about process, not power. Ask, how does a purchase like this usually get approved here? And, apart from you, who else will be involved?
Asking, are you the decision-maker, can embarrass people. And never go to the managing director behind your contact's back. Ask your contact to introduce you.
Sales maths
Plan backwards from your target
Target / average deal = wins needed
Wins / win rate = qualified opportunities
Divide by 12 for each month
Coverage needed = 1 / your win rate
Only count qualified opportunities, never every name you messaged.
For example, Ifeoma runs a staff training business in Lagos. Her target is 18,000,000 naira of new contracts in 12 months, and her average deal is 1,500,000. So she needs 12 wins.
Her win rate on qualified opportunities is 25%. So she needs 12 divided by 0.25, which is 48 qualified opportunities.
That is 4 new qualified opportunities every month, about one a week.
With a 25% win rate she needs 4 times coverage: pipeline worth 4 times what she must close this quarter.
A qualified opportunity has a real need, a conversation with someone in the decision, and a realistic path to purchase. Counting unqualified names is the most common way sellers fool themselves.
Choosing accounts
Your ideal customer profile
Sector
Size that drives your price
Location you can serve well
Situation: the likely problem
Ability to pay
An ideal customer profile describes the organisations that get the most value from you. Write down their sector, and the size measure that drives your price, like staff or beds.
Add the location you can serve well, and the situation, the problem they are likely to have.
And their ability to pay.
Then look for buying signals: a new branch, a new managing director, a new regulation, or a job advert for the very role you support.
Score 1 to 5 on each criterion
Multiply by weights that add to 100%
4.0 and above: Tier 1
3.0 to 3.9: Tier 2, below: Tier 3
For example, Halima sells IT support to private healthcare in Abuja. She scores each account from 1 to 5 on fit, signs of need, access and ability to pay.
Fit weighs 40%, need 30%, access and ability to pay 15% each.
Hospital B, opening a second branch, scores 4.55. Clinic E, advertising for an IT officer, scores 4.15. Both are Tier 1 and get personal effort this month.
Lab C and hospital D score 3.4, so they are Tier 2. Clinic A scores 2.7, Tier 3 for now. Keep Tier 1 short, and re-score every three months.
Key points
Remember
A group decides; find each role
Approval limits show who really signs
Target / deal size = wins; wins / win rate = opportunities
Use your own numbers and honest definitions
A short, scored Tier 1 list beats a long one

To remember. A group decides, so find each role. Approval limits show who really signs. Plan backwards from your target, with your own honest numbers. And a short, scored Tier 1 list beats a long generic one.

Account plan
What goes on one page
Spend about an hour on research: the website, annual reports, the CAC public search, LinkedIn, job adverts and tender notices. Write the key facts, recent signals, and the buying group.
The most important line is the value hypothesis: your best guess, in numbers, of what the problem costs them. It is a guess to test, never a fact to present.
Add likely alternatives, and your next three actions with dates. Gaps are fine. They become your discovery questions.
Worked example
Ngozi's value hypothesis
About 40 trucks
2 lost days a truck each month
40 x 2 = 80 truck-days lost
A hypothesis is a question to test, not a claim.
For example, Ngozi sells fleet maintenance scheduling. Her Tier 1 account is a haulage company in Kano with about 40 trucks.
She guesses each truck loses about 2 days a month to unplanned breakdowns.
That is 80 truck-days lost each month.
If one truck-day earns about 150,000 naira, still to confirm, that is 12,000,000 naira of revenue at risk a month.
In the meeting she asks, how many days a month are trucks off the road unexpectedly? If the true number is lower, she revises the plan instead of pushing a weak case.

MEDDICC is a private checklist of seven things to know. Metrics: the result the buyer wants, in their own numbers. And the economic buyer, who releases the money.
Decision criteria: what they will judge suppliers on.
Decision process: the steps, people and dates to a signature.
Identify pain: why it matters now, and what happens if nothing changes.
Champion: who inside wants you to win and has influence.
Competition, including doing nothing. Score each letter known, partly known or unknown. At negotiation, an unknown economic buyer or no champion means real risk.
Mutual action plan
Work backwards from go-live
Every open deal needs a next step with a date the buyer agreed.
For example, Amina's champion wants her payroll service live for the March payroll on 25 March. She works backwards with him. Dates are illustrative.
A demo to finance on 22 January, then the business case review on 5 February.
Managing director approval by 12 February, so the contract is signed by 19 February. That leaves time to load 180 staff records and run a side-by-side test.
Each step has an owner. When the IT check slipped a week, the HR manager pushed it himself, because it threatened his own goal.
If there is no measurable pain, no access to an approver, or no agreed next step, close the deal politely. A clean pipeline gives a true forecast.

Stay honest and safe
Three habits that protect trust
Never call hopeful deals commit, or hide likely deals to look good later.
Ask buyers for 15 minutes of honest feedback. Record fixed reason codes.
Collect only work details you need, protect your CRM, never buy lists, honour opt-outs.
Report what the evidence supports. Inflating and sandbagging both make planning impossible for the people who depend on your numbers.
After each decision, ask for 15 minutes of feedback. For example, if 8 of Ifeoma's 14 losses were no decision, her real competitor is the status quo, not price.
And contact details are personal data under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Use two-step login, never buy or share lists, and remove anyone who asks you to stop.

SPIN discovery
Four kinds of question
Problem: difficulties
SPIN was developed by Neil Rackham and the Huthwaite team after observing more than 35,000 business-to-business sales interactions.
Situation questions find facts you could not research. Keep them few, because they bore senior people.
Problem questions find difficulties. Where does the current setup cause the most trouble?
Implication questions explore the consequences. They are the heart of a complex sale, because most buyers have never added up what a problem costs.
Need-payoff questions let the buyer say what solving it would be worth. When they work out the cost themselves, the figure belongs to them.
Worked example
Putting a number on outages
Down about 3 times a month, 4 hours each
3 x 4 = 12 hours of downtime
12 x 250,000 = 3,000,000 naira on paper
About 10% never collected: 3,600,000 a year
Never inflate numbers. If the buyer's estimate is small, accept it.
For example, Halima sells IT support. At Hospital B, the IT officer says the system goes down about 3 times a month, for about 4 hours each time.
That is 12 hours of downtime a month. She asks, what happens to billing then?
The finance manager says the desk handles about 250,000 naira of bills an hour, written on paper during outages. So about 3,000,000 naira a month goes the paper route.
He estimates about 10% is never collected. That is 300,000 naira a month, or 3,600,000 a year. These are the hospital's own estimates.
Implication questions help buyers see real costs. Never use them to frighten people. A case built on inflated numbers collapses when finance checks it.
Within 24 hours, send a written recap and invite corrections.
Business case
Halima's case for Hospital B
For example, Halima proposes IT support at 350,000 naira a month, plus 600,000 naira setup.
Year-one cost
Total yearly benefit
Net year-one gain
Figures are illustrative.
Finance looks for three numbers: total cost, return on investment, and payback.
For example, Halima proposes 350,000 naira a month, plus a one-time setup of 600,000.
Year one costs 4,800,000 naira.
The benefits, using the hospital's own estimates, are recovered billing, fewer emergency callouts, and less overtime. Together, about 5,880,000 naira.
That is a net gain of 1,080,000 naira, a return of 22.5%. Payback comes during month 5.
She also shows a cautious case. If only 40% of billing is recovered, year one shows a loss. Showing that honestly made her proposal more credible, not less.
Negotiation
Answering a discount request
Before negotiating, write your BATNA, your best alternative if this deal fails, plus your ideal outcome and walk-away point.
Procurement asks Halima for 10% off. Over a year that is 420,000 naira given away for nothing.
Instead she asks what is driving the request. The budget line is tight. So she offers 5% off, if the hospital signs for 24 months and pays within 14 days.
Procurement gets a saving to report, and Halima gets two years of work and faster payment.
Stay safe
Protect yourself and your money
Never offer gifts, cash or a percentage to influence a purchase. Walk away if one is requested.
Confirm tenders on the buyer's official website or published number. Never pay to receive a contract.
Verify the company, speak to past staff, get the plan in writing. Never pay a fee to start.
Stay clean in procurement. Never offer gifts, cash or a percentage to anyone to influence a purchase, and walk away if one is requested.
Beware of fake tender notices and registration fees sent from personal email accounts. Confirm on the buyer's official website, and never pay to receive a contract.
Be careful with commission-only offers from companies you cannot verify, and with any role that asks you to pay a fee to start.
Your career
Read a commission plan carefully
OTE: base plus target commission
Accelerator: higher rate above quota
Clawback: when you must return pay
Paid on signed contracts or cash?
On-target earnings are base pay plus target commission. For example, Bisi is offered 400,000 naira base and 200,000 target commission a month. That is 600,000 naira a month.
Above quota, an accelerator pays a higher rate. Beating her quarterly quota by 3,000,000 naira lifts her commission from 600,000 to 840,000.
A clawback is commission you return if a client cancels or does not pay.
And check whether commission is paid on signed contracts or on cash collected. Run your own numbers at 80%, 100% and 120% of quota before you accept.
